en: Sarybai stood there raging,
Armed with all his weapons,
Upon the broad plain of Kosh-Töbö.
The people clashed amid a great outcry
Upon the field of battle;
Those who boasted of strength and valor
Lost heart and bowed,
While my champions and lions
Despaired of their wretched lives.
“Such is Sarybai;
He has waged the battle relentlessly.
Whenever the madman moves,
He slaughters multitudes of us.
Against this infidel Sarybai,
Can any man’s strength prevail?
Can even a lion’s fang pierce him?
For us to regain peace,
When will this swine ever die?
He has emptied the land and slaughtered the people;
On what blessed day will dawn break,
And when will God deliver us?”
Pining away in anguish,
The people despaired of life;
The savagery of the boar
Who devastated the nation was revealed.
Wildly exulting, he roared,
“Who will come out to single combat?”
And called forth in fury.
He urged on Too-Kyzyl beneath him,
Making the horse stride ponderously;
A grievous sight even to contemplate,
He threw the whole world into panic.
Raising the clamor of bloody slaughter,
Enshrouding the wondrous mountains in haze,
Your infidel, vast as Mount Kap,
Armed himself and came out to fight.
The infidel Khan Sarybai
Shot and hacked through the battle;
The people panicked, unable to prevail,
And despaired of their mortal lives;
Unable to find their bearings, they fled.
When strong men’s backs were broken,
When he slaughtered all who faced him,
They fought but could not prevail;
Six times before this
They had battled without defeating him.
The poor people merely watched;
Whenever Sarybai entered the field,
The nation cried out in anguish,
Despairing of their fly-like lives.
Their courage failed and they cringed,
Wondering how many souls would be slaughtered;
Their sight dimmed and their eyes bulged
Whenever Sarybai entered the fray.
The people wailed in misery,
And languished beneath their punishment.
Against Sarybai’s venom
No human strength prevailed;
He was like the wrath of the true God,
The very image of a death-defying man,
Fierce in anger and mighty in venom,
With the black eyes of a fiend.
The people despaired of life;
Already timid, the poor folk
Grew sallow as in a wasting sickness.
They spoke together in whispers;
The poor people were crushed,
Unable to find their bearings.
Against the infidel warrior Sarybai,
Not one soul could venture forth.
The whole world was stricken with fear,
And every counsel was exhausted;
All the warriors stood helpless,
Wondering whence this monster’s son,
This infidel, had sprung.
“Which broad-necked young warrior
Will go out to face him alone?
Who will dare encounter him in battle?
Who can fathom the measure
Of this thousandfold courageous scourge?
Who, experienced and wise among the people,
Will go against this infidel Sarybai
With keen judgment?
Which great champion called a lion
Will answer his challenge with skill?
Murapy, auspicious when he raises the war cry,
Whose shout is like a thousand warriors—
Will he perhaps go?
Whoever faces him will die.”
The heroes despaired of life,
And the people crowded together, lamenting;
The entire army cried aloud.
“Warriors Seytek and Külchoro,
Unless you find some means,
Death has stalked us down;
Every expedient is utterly gone.
Can anyone match him in battle?
Can any man overcome him in combat?
Can anyone advance against him?
Can one who meets him remain alive?
How can we gain deliverance
From this black-fiendish swine?
When he rages in fury,
Even another madman like me
Will meet a death of bitter doom;
Many men who go out singly
Will be encircled and captured.”
The people despaired of life,
Their senses reeling and their strength gone;
No words remained for them to say.
What calamity was this, what deed,
Whose outcome none could foresee?
While his people grieved,
There was one lion devoted to his nation,
A hero born to heroic fortune,
A tempered blade of black steel.
Have you not heard the tidings
Of that noble lion’s descendant?
Famed and mighty in wrath,
He was the magnanimous hero’s son;
Those who once defied him were hewn down,
And hostile enemies were slaughtered.
His forefather before his father
Had received a blessing from Babadin;
He was called the son of a warrior lion.
Each time he dwindled, he blazed anew;
Each time he died, he multiplied.
God prospered all his deeds,
And the Forty Holy Ones and Khizr Ilyas
Accompanied and sustained him.
The hero-born warrior Seytek,
A mighty youth built like an elephant,
Had stirred a vast commotion throughout the world;
A warrior in courage, with a heart of stone,
A leopard blessed with surpassing fortune,
He was a saint born but once
Into this deceitful world.
His racehorse was Kulansur—
Not Kulansur, but Kuyunsur,
A rare gray steed born once in an age,
Which his fairy maternal ancestors
Had presented to him as a gift.
With flowing forelock and full mane,
The creature was magnificent;
Noble-backed and gentle-tempered,
It never wearied when ridden over hills,
Never tired in battle,
Never flagged on a distant ride,
And never flinched when ridden into combat:
A dark bay battle horse,
With sieve-like lungs and copper wings,
Its bit like a polished lance,
Its darting motion like a snake,
Its speed like a wild ass.
God Almighty fashions
Living creatures in every kind.
Broad in the chest and narrow behind—
Such was the racehorse Kulansur.
Upon that swift Kulansur
Were laid a leather saddlecloth and blue saddle,
A white felt pad beneath,
All fitted upon Kulansur.
More skillful than the most accomplished,
A friend of the prophet David,
The master Bölökbai of the Forty Kalmyks
Had fashioned your noble hero’s white saddle
In exquisite beauty.
Its pommel was white gold,
Its cantle solid silver,
And both sides were broad iron;
It did not pitch him forward on a slope.
Into the golden-soled stirrups
The noble lion, dearer than a father,
Leapt without touching them and sped away.
His lionhood stood revealed
As he mounted and galloped;
His eyes flashed, burning like fire,
And he sharpened his tongue like a millstone.
His courage and lionheartedness
Showed in his singular bearing;
The hearts of all who watched him
Surged and leapt within them.
Taking courage and receiving their blessing,
He set forth in valor.
Such was that noble lion,
That gallant hero, proud as a cock.
To face bloodshed, courage, and mighty strife,
To test himself in combat,
He fixed his gaze on Sarybai,
On the wrathful and venomous one,
On that thick-armed champion,
That black fiendish warrior
Who scattered peoples and ruined nations.
He went to taste his true torment,
And, if true death had come, to die.
He summoned stern resolve;
The young lion, that noble champion,
The warrior Seytek, staked
His precious life upon a hair.
Esteeming himself able and lionhearted,
He went against the furious foe,
To shed blood and take life
And clash against him,
To die if true death had arrived.
Boasting of courage and lionhood,
Boasting of strength and valor,
He went to settle the account
Of the infidel Sarybai.
He went to begin the strife and break the host,
To be struck by a musket ball and fall,
To perish and die,
To grapple and contend,
And spill without mercy the blood
Of the oppressor who brought lamentation;
To strike and raise the conflict,
And deliver the poor people, once living free,
From this fevered, calamitous war,
And bring them safely away.
The young lion and tiger
Revealed himself a true champion;
He donned his coat no bullet could pierce,
Flicked his eyelids and arched his brows,
And the noble tiger showed no concern.
He did not esteem the monster’s son,
That swine, worth even his boot-heel;
He reckoned him less than a hair and never flinched,
Never stirred in apprehension.
Turning toward the qibla,
He lifted the enchanted spear inherited from his fathers
And aimed it toward the enemy.
With Zulfiqar fastened at his waist,
He invoked the spirits
Of his forefathers who had passed before.
When the gray-maned wolf rode forth,
Ancestral spirits settled upon him in majesty;
He towered like a lofty mountain,
Appearing like a blue-ridged peak,
And all who saw him felt their hearts stirred.
He girded on his fearsome steel
And prepared for the combat,
Calling upon the spirit
Of the magnanimous hero gone to the next world.
The descendant of the sovereign lion
Looked neither up nor down,
And counted the calamity of death
As no more than a hair.
When one gazed at him, the heart was stirred;
If six great rivers turned,
They seemed no more than a cleft in the earth;
The confluence of six streams
Seemed no more than a mountain pass.
When the noble lion grew wrathful,
He seemed able to engulf the whole world;
Even the vast, broad-breasted earth
Seemed unable to withstand
The prince’s valiant son.
